source: Pontis & Blandford (2016) Understanding 'Influence': An empirical test of the data-frame theory of sensemaking
finding: One of few direct tests of the data/frame model on a new task type (structure tasks, not stories). Most D/F activities appeared, but three did not.
numbers: 11 participants (6 HCI master's students as novices, 5 staff with 10+ years as experts), 44 tasks in all. Activities not observed: seeking and inferring new relationships, tracking anomalies, seeking a new frame.
limits: Tiny qualitative sample, coded by the authors, one domain pair (HCI vs chemistry). Not a quantitative test; it extends the model rather than confirming it.
agent_relevance: The model's reframe step (O8) may be rare in tasks that have no story to break. Do not assume reframing occurs by default.

source: Pontis & Blandford (2016) Understanding 'Influence': An empirical test of the data-frame theory of sensemaking (frame count)
finding: In every one of 44 tasks, people kept a single frame and elaborated it. They did not hold or compare rival frames, though the D/F model says people can compare frames.
numbers: 44 of 44 tasks: one frame only.
quote: participants only worked with one frame
limits: Structure tasks with open web search; may differ from time-pressured field work.
agent_relevance: Single-frame commitment is the human default. An agent that holds several frames at once is doing something humans mostly do not.

source: Pontis & Blandford (2016) Understanding 'Influence': An empirical test of the data-frame theory of sensemaking (expertise)
finding: Experts relied on prior knowledge (soft evidence) and explored more before choosing; novices wanted hard evidence and decided in shorter journeys with arbitrary picks. Experts elaborated the initial frame and checked source quality more.
numbers: Example journeys: novice N6 had 6 data points, expert E2 had 15 data points, with more discarded by E2.
limits: Two example journeys out of 11 people; 'expert' means 5+ years in both research and domain.
agent_relevance: Frame quality depends on stored domain knowledge. A scaffold cannot replace missing domain knowledge; it can only force the check steps experts do.

source: Pontis & Blandford (2016) Understanding 'Influence': An empirical test of the data-frame theory of sensemaking (new activities)
finding: The authors had to add activities the model lacks: pre-selecting candidates and making a final decision. Quality and plausibility checks appeared as frequent explicit steps.
numbers: Added: preselection of candidates and final decision (activity 5h in their figure).
limits: Authors' own coding scheme; two coders compared logs.
agent_relevance: Supports a separate plausibility and source-check step in S2 before any frame is kept.

source: Klein, Jalaeian, Hoffman, Mueller (2023) The plausibility transition model for sensemaking
finding: The data/frame authors' own successor. Sensemaking is a story built from state transitions, judged for plausibility, and stops when the story feels plausible enough. Built from cases, not experiments.
numbers: 1,042 articles screened, 22 kept; 73-case corpus (convenience sample); 23 cases analysed, all by one coder (senior author). AF447, USS Vincennes, Waco, AlphaGo, Royal Majesty among the cases. Zero experiments.
quote: Our notion of plausibility is psychological, not philosophical, linguistic or computational.
limits: No inter-rater check; imagined-protagonist method is hard to replicate; two authors work at a firm that sells related training. Three predictions (individual differences, abrupt gap closure, gap detection follows story transitions) are untested.
agent_relevance: Shows the original model is still evidence by case study. Treat its claims as design hypotheses to test on our agent, not as established effects.

source: Klein, Moon, Hoffman (2006) Making sense of sensemaking 2: a macrocognitive model
finding: Original statement of the data/frame model. Catalog record lists five empirical areas it reviews: causal reasoning, commitment to hypotheses, feedback and learning, sensemaking as a skill, confirmation bias. Full text not reachable this session.
numbers: No numbers read.
limits: Only the record and a search summary were seen; the full paper was blocked.
agent_relevance: Baseline claim set; mark every empirical claim from it as unread until the PDF is opened.

source: Lehner, Adelman, Cheikes, Brown (2008) Confirmation bias in complex analyses (MITRE report 04-0985 version)
finding: From a search summary: confirmation bias appeared in both analyst and non-analyst groups, and Analysis of Competing Hypotheses reduced it only for people without intelligence experience. The bias showed as a weighting effect, not an interpretation effect.
numbers: No exact figures read (PDF blocked with 403).
limits: Secondhand summary only. A later MITRE remote-sensing study and a UK experiment reportedly found ACH effects not robust (also unread).
agent_relevance: Structured alternative-listing helps novices more than experts; do the evidence weighting in code, since the bias sits in weighting.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR 2024), oracle labels
finding: Earlier self-correction gains came from using the true answer to decide when to stop. With oracle labels, accuracy rises; this is not real revision.
numbers: Accuracy standard vs oracle self-correct. GPT-3.5: GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 to 29.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 to 97.5, CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 to 59.0.
quote: these results can only be regarded as indicative of an oracle's performance.
limits: Table was read from a text extraction with interleaved labels; row pairing inferred. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 only in this table.
agent_relevance: Matches G2: revise only from a real external signal. Own opinion of the frame is not a signal.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet, intrinsic self-correction
finding: Without labels, asking the model to re-examine its own answer lowered accuracy on nearly every benchmark. The model changes right answers to wrong more often than the reverse.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after round 1 and 41.8 after round 2; GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7; HotpotQA 26.0 to 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0; CommonSenseQA 82.0 to 79.5 to 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 to 49.0 to 43.0. GPT-3.5 kept its first GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time.
limits: 2023-era models; GPT-4-Turbo and Llama-2 also dropped. Newer reasoning models not tested. Prompts were generic 'review your answer'.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a scheduled 'rethink the frame' step can hurt. Reframe (O8) must fire on a signal only (G1).

source: Huang et al. (2024) cannot self-correct reasoning yet, voting comparison
finding: With a matched number of responses, plain self-consistency voting beat multi-agent debate on GSM8K. Debate gain is mostly from sampling many answers.
numbers: GSM8K with GPT-3.5: self-consistency reached 88.2 at 9 responses; debate was lower (about 83.0 at 9) per the garbled table.
limits: Table values read from a garbled extraction; use direction, not decimals.
agent_relevance: Debate between frames from one model adds little beyond samples; supports G4.

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville (2025) LLMs get lost in multi-turn conversation
finding: When information arrives in pieces, 15 models do much worse than when given it all at once. They guess early, build on the guess, and do not recover. This is a live test of frame fixation in LLMs.
numbers: Average drop of 39% over six tasks; 200,000+ simulated conversations; 15 LLMs from 8 families. Aptitude fell 16%, unreliability rose 112%. Same text given at once (CONCAT) scored 95.1% of full, so information loss is not the cause.
quote: when LLMs take a wrong turn in a conversation, they get lost and do not recover.
limits: Simulated user (GPT-4o-mini) and sharded instructions (90-120 per task); tasks are generation, not diagnosis. Temperature 1 by default.
agent_relevance: Strongest LLM evidence that an early assumption becomes a frame the model will not drop. Keep early hypotheses marked as provisional and re-derive from all data.

source: Laban et al. (2025) Lost in conversation, reasoning models and fixes
finding: Extra reasoning did not fix it. Restating all prior information helped only part way.
numbers: o3 and DeepSeek-R1 degraded like others; reasoning models wrote answers 33% longer, and longer answers held more assumptions. SNOWBALL (repeat all earlier shards each turn) recovered 15-20% of the drop; RECAP at the last turn recovered more but is unrealistic.
limits: Recap tests used only GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini on four tasks.
agent_relevance: Re-presenting the full data each step (a rebuilt state, not a running chat) is a cheap partial fix. Code should rebuild the context, not rely on chat history.

source: Laban et al. (2025) Lost in conversation, premature answer attempts
finding: The appendix measures when the first answer attempt appears in the conversation, since early attempts are the mechanism of the failure.
numbers: Binned by conversation progress (0-20% to 80-100%); one model row shows 33.3 to 69.3 across bins in the appendix table.
limits: Number read from a partial table extraction; exact link between bin and accuracy not fully read.
agent_relevance: Delay committing a frame until enough cues are in; count cues in code, not by model judgement.

source: Zheng, Miller, Bialkowski, Soyer, Janda (2025) Supporting data-frame dynamics in AI-assisted decision making
finding: Workshop paper that formalises the data/frame model for human-AI teams: evidence extraction, hypothesis retrieval, and hypothesis scoring, shown only as a skin-cancer prototype. No user study.
numbers: Six pages; no measured results.
limits: Position paper; concept bottleneck model, not an LLM test.
agent_relevance: A usable formal skeleton for S2: extract evidence, retrieve frames, score each, with human override. No evidence yet that it helps.

source: Position paper (2026) From sycophancy to sensemaking
finding: Casts sensemaking as a control loop: a break between expected and observed is the error signal, and revision should repair the premise that broke. Proposes premise status (draft, contested, committed, rejected) and typed routing: goal break to reframe, evidence break to investigate, process break to negotiate.
numbers: Counts only: 3 discrepancy types, 4 premise statuses, 3 guarantees, 3 untested predictions. No experiments.
quote: progress occurs when evidence repairs the specific premise that broke.
limits: No empirical test at all; one tutoring scenario.
agent_relevance: Design idea for O8: store each frame premise with a status and route by what broke. Mark it untested.

source: Huang et al. (2026) Understanding the anchoring effect of LLM with synthetic data (SynAnchors)
finding: Anchoring on first information is common in LLMs: 22 to 61% of questions are anchored. Reasoning models are mildest, not immune.
numbers: SynAnchors: 60 semantic questions over 10 topics plus 40 numeric questions over 10 topics; 30 samples per question. Total anchored ratio: Qwen2.5-0.5B 60.5%, Phi-3.5-mini 46.3%, Qwen2.5-7B 40.0%, GPT-4o-mini 37.0%, GPT-4o 27.3%, DeepSeek-R1 25.0%, Qwen3-235B thinking 22.0%.
limits: Small synthetic set (100 questions); some entries blank in extraction; judgments, not diagnosis.
agent_relevance: The first frame offered pulls later judgment even in the best models. Do not put a leading frame in the prompt before cues are listed.

source: Huang et al. (2026) SynAnchors, mitigation tests
finding: Common fixes did not remove anchoring. Reasoning was the best mitigation; a two-phase prompt (set your own standard first) helped one model only.
numbers: Llama-3.1-8B total ratio 34.7% base; question-aware prompt 36.8%; knowledge enhancement 50.5%; self-improving 38.4%; adversarial finetuning 33.3%; DoLa 37.5-38.5%; Anti-DP 24.7%. Qwen2.5-7B base 40.0%; Anti-DP 40.8%, self-improving 48.0%.
limits: Two small models; ratios based on 30 samples per question and 100 questions.
agent_relevance: Self-review prompts can raise bias (self-improving made Qwen worse). Supports G1 and G2.

source: Huang et al. (2026) SynAnchors, mechanism
finding: Activation patching finds anchoring acts in shallow layers; reasoning traces mention the anchor less as they go, which suggests other information dilutes it.
numbers: Qualitative proportions of anchor mentions in reasoning traces (their Figure 3); no single effect size read.
limits: Correlation in traces; traces are not a faithful record of the decision.
agent_relevance: Longer evidence-gathering before commitment may dilute first-cue pull; test it on our agent.

source: Shaikh, Dandekar et al. (2024) CBEval: evaluating and interpreting cognitive biases in LLMs
finding: Five biases (framing, round-number, anchoring, representativeness, priming) probed on GPT-4o and others with Shapley attribution of prompt words. Mostly case demonstrations.
numbers: Few counts; example: GPT-4o and Llama 3.1 gave the right count of 3 despite a planted wrong count of 4 in a persuasion prompt. Models preferred a score of 65 out of 100.
limits: Independent authors; small prompt sets; no effect sizes or sample counts; weak evidence.
agent_relevance: Low weight. Useful only as a reminder that framing words change choice.

source: Early diagnostic commitment in LLM clinical reasoning (NeurIPS 2026 submission)
finding: In reasoning traces, the model's final diagnosis is often fixed well before the trace ends, and the rest of the text keeps listing alternatives without changing the outcome.
numbers: 8 open reasoning models; 1,146 base traces, 1.7 million resampled traces; 36% commit before halfway, 61% before three-quarters; 96.1% of traces put top probability on the diagnosis they finally give.
limits: Abstract page only; open models; MedQA, MedMCQA and NEJM CPC vignettes; commitment defined by total variation distance on resamples.
agent_relevance: Shows that written 'consider alternatives' text can be decoration. Verify a frame change by resampling, not by reading the trace.

source: Quantifying and mitigating premature closure in frontier LLMs (2026)
finding: When the right option was removed, models still gave an answer most of the time. A short safety prompt cut it by about a third but not to zero.
numbers: 5 models; MedQA 500 items (250 answerable), AfriMed-QA 490. Baseline false-action about 70% (range 55-81%); with prompt about 48%. HealthBench subset 861 questions: premature closure 20.7-44.6% baseline; red-team 191 queries: 59.3-91.4%. Answerable-item accuracy fell about 1.0 point.
limits: Two LLM judges (kappa 0.685); no multiple-comparison correction; simple prompt only.
agent_relevance: A frame-fit check must allow 'none of these fits'. Include an explicit no-fit exit.

source: Same facts, different diagnosis: narrative anchoring (2026 preprint)
finding: The same medical facts told in a different voice lowered accuracy. Rewriting the story into a clinical voice helped most; extracting facts into a fixed record helped the gap but lowered overall accuracy.
numbers: 12 open models (3B-24B); 1,000 MedQA vignettes, 3 voices each. Accuracy 0.635 (clinical) vs 0.546 and 0.531; pooled penalty minus 9.6 points. Chain-of-thought gap 0.090 vs 0.098 direct (not significant per model). Debias instruction cut gap 14%. Rewrite-then-reason gap 0.047, significant in 8 of 11 models, but broke 19.8% of correct items. Schema extraction lowered overall accuracy 4.9 points.
quote: The representation a model reasons over matters more than how much it reasons.
limits: Generation temperature differed across voices; synthetic voices; one rewriter; models up to 24B.
agent_relevance: How cues are worded sets the frame. Normalising cues to a neutral form before framing works, but extraction can drop facts; keep the original available.

source: Language models keep abandoned analyses: residue after garden-path sentences (2026)
finding: After a reading is disproved, 24 models still carry a trace of it: later text is pulled toward the abandoned parse. A corrected value still pulls later predictions.
numbers: 24 open models, 124M to 70B; residue about three-quarters of a true-object effect; corrected statement still pulls in 8 of 9 models; activation patching removes almost all residue in the 32B and 70B models.
limits: Abstract page only; syntax task, not decision task; open models.
agent_relevance: Evidence that dropped frames leave residue. After a reframe, rebuild the context without the discarded frame instead of saying 'ignore that'.

source: Failing to falsify: confirmation bias in language models (2026)
finding: On a 2-4-6 style rule-discovery task, LLMs mostly test cases that fit their guess, so they find the rule less often. Telling them to look for counterexamples helps.
numbers: 11 LLMs; average rule-discovery rate rose from 42% to 56% (14 points) with counterexample prompts; distilled behaviour transferred to a Blicket task (no numbers on the page).
limits: Abstract only; models not named; one task family.
agent_relevance: Support for a code-forced 'test what would break this frame' step in S2, since a prompt alone moved results only 14 points.

source: Wild guesses and mild guesses in active concept learning (2026)
finding: A rival view: positive-test (confirm-leaning) queries are not simply a flaw. Information-maximising queries win on compound rules but fail when the LLM proposes invalid programs; positive tests converge faster on simple rules.
numbers: Number Game; no numbers on the abstract page.
limits: Abstract only; one task; neuro-symbolic learner.
agent_relevance: Falsification is not always better; use it when the first frame fails or stays ambiguous, not on every step.

source: Belief perseverance (encyclopedia summary of Ross, Anderson and others)
finding: Beliefs persist after the evidence behind them is withdrawn. This page reports only a sphere-volume study and a calculator study, not the original debriefing numbers.
numbers: Sphere study: 19 scientists, 18 kept using a spurious formula. Calculator study: about half kept believing.
limits: Secondary page; the original debriefing papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: Human frames persist after support is gone. A frame must be tied to its supporting cues so removing the cues removes the frame.

source: Lord, Lepper & Preston (1984) Considering the opposite (from memory)
finding: Asking people to consider the opposite reduced biased assimilation more than asking them to be fair. Recalled from background knowledge, not read here.
numbers: Not read; no figures recorded.
limits: Unverified this session. Later work found mixed durability.
agent_relevance: The consider-the-opposite prompt has human backing but is not LLM-tested here; test before relying on it.

source: Tolcott, Marvin & Lehner (1989) Effects of early decisions on later judgments (from memory)
finding: Intelligence analysts who committed early to a hypothesis weighted later evidence in its favour. Recalled from background knowledge, not read.
numbers: Not read; no figures recorded.
limits: Unverified; cited as the sort of early-commitment effect the data/frame model describes.
agent_relevance: Background for the fixation risk the scaffold must handle.
